Title: The Benedictine Codex

It was the first snowstorm of December when the bells of St. Anselm’s Monastery rang out of rhythm — not the usual measured peal of Matins, but the sharp clang of alarm.

The Codex Benedictus, the monastery’s most treasured illuminated manuscript, had vanished.

The manuscript had been kept in the scriptorium’s secure archive, a chamber cut from solid stone, with no windows and only one heavy oak door. The door had been locked and sealed the night before by Brother Alaric, the librarian, who kept the only key — which he wore around his neck even as he slept in the adjoining cell. A novice had stood watch in the hallway all night outside the door. The lock was intact, the seals unbroken, and yet: the codex was gone by Lauds.

As the monks clustered in the cloister, murmuring beneath the snow-heavy sky, it was not the Prior or the sub-Prior who began to ask the right questions. It was Brother Gregory — the cook.

No one paid much attention to Gregory. He was plump, ruddy, and fond of humming little tunes as he stirred endless pots of porridge. But he had a quiet habit of observation. He noticed what was eaten, and what was not. And that morning, something was off.

First, Brother Thomas hadn’t touched the blackberry compote. Odd, since he usually asked for seconds. Brother Alaric, meanwhile, requested mint tea instead of his usual strong black brew. And Brother Guillaume, who claimed to have spent the night fasting in the chapel, had blisters on his lips.

Gregory said nothing, not yet. Instead, after the meal, he made his way to the archive with Prior Matthias and the others, who were pacing and pointing endlessly at the unbroken seals, the single door, the unyielding walls.

“It was locked all night!” Brother Alaric said for the fifth time. “I wore the key around my neck. I slept like any other night. No one entered.”

“Who had access to the key before it was locked?” Gregory asked mildly.

“No one,” Alaric said. “Only me. I locked the door myself just after Compline.”

“And the codex — remind me, what was it bound in?”

“Vellum and oak boards, with silver clasps.”

“Thick, then,” Gregory mused. “Bulky.”

“Yes. One couldn’t hide it under a robe.”

Brother Guillaume scoffed. “Is this really the time to discuss breakfast and bindings?”

But Gregory only smiled. “Tell me, Guillaume — where were you last night?”

“I told you,” Guillaume huffed. “Praying in the chapel.”

“Fasting?”

“Yes, all night.”

“Strange,” Gregory said. “Because your lips are blistered, as though from heat.”

Guillaume touched his mouth instinctively.

“And Alaric,” Gregory continued, his tone still pleasant, “you’re fond of black coffee. Yet today you asked for mint tea.”

“I wasn’t feeling well,” Alaric replied, looking startled.

“I imagine not,” Gregory said. “Inhaling smoke will do that.”

He turned to the prior. “May I see the kitchen hearth?”

Perplexed, Prior Matthias led him to the scullery. Gregory moved a few logs aside and lifted the iron ash pan beneath. Sifting carefully through layers of gray soot, he retrieved a charred shard of oak — with a sliver of silver still attached.

“Here is your codex,” he said softly.

A gasp swept the room.

“But—but how?” Alaric stammered. “The door was locked! The key never left my neck!”

“It never needed to,” Gregory said. “You locked the room, yes. But before you did, you hid the manuscript inside the hearth flue of your room, knowing that your wall adjoins the archive. A loose stone — perhaps recently repaired — granted access to the archive side of the wall. Once the room was ‘secure,’ you waited for Guillaume to retrieve the codex through the flue, pass it to the kitchen, and burn it before morning. The snowstorm was your ally: smoke would vanish into the blizzard, and no one would be wiser.”

“Why?” the prior whispered.

“The abbot of Sainte-Marie offered us five thousand francs if we 'loaned' it long-term,” Guillaume spat. “Alaric and I planned to fake a theft. But the storm ruined everything. There was no way to sneak it out. And once it was gone, we panicked.”

“Panicked badly enough,” Gregory said, “that Guillaume blistered himself feeding the fire too high, and Alaric lost his taste for coffee.”

Brother Alaric sagged where he stood. The key around his neck glinted like an accusation.

Gregory bowed slightly. “Breakfast is a mirror of the soul, Prior. People forget their habits when they are hiding something.”

And with that, he returned to the kitchen, humming softly, already considering what to cook for supper.

The Slightest Difference

It began with the junk drawer.

Marjorie had opened it a thousand times. It was the bottom right drawer in the kitchen, the one that caught slightly on the frame unless you lifted it just so. She wasn’t even thinking about it when she tugged it open to grab the scissors. But tonight, May 17th, a Tuesday, the drawer slid out easily. Smoother than it should have.

She stood for a moment, scissors in hand.

She tried pushing the drawer shut and pulling it again. No catch. Smooth. Silent. As if someone had sanded the raw edge and oiled the runners.

She supposed she could have done that herself and forgotten. Maybe a weekend project? It wasn't the sort of thing you'd remember. Still, she had a memory—faint but definite—of grumbling about that drawer just a few days ago, wrestling it for a roll of tape.

She let it go.

Later that evening, she walked down the hallway with her tea, lights dimmed, the house quiet the way she liked it. Outside, the night pressed gently against the windows, soft and formless. She paused at the hallway mirror, fussing with her hair. It was an antique mirror, a little warped, inherited from her aunt, and the reflection always shimmered around the edges like water. She leaned in to inspect a gleam of silver at her temples.

Her reflection blinked.

Not wrong. Not late. But not quite right either. The blink happened in time, just slightly off. Not a half-second—less than that, but unmistakable. Like a dubbed movie just slightly out of sync.

She leaned closer. Stared. Her reflection stared back, perfectly matched. She raised her hand. So did the image. No delay, no error. She watched for a full minute.

She shook her head and laughed under her breath. She was tired. She’d been under stress lately. Little things seemed bigger when you were stretched thin.

She turned and walked into the bedroom.

The door closed behind her, as it always did — except this time, the hinge was on the opposite side.

She froze.

It was identical in every other way. Same woodgrain, same brass handle with the tiny pockmark near the base. Same squeak at the midpoint. But the swing was reversed. She opened it again. Closed it. Each time it swung left instead of right.

Marjorie sat down on the edge of the bed. She looked around.

Nothing else had changed.

Nothing obvious.

She walked through the house slowly, turning on lights. She opened cupboards. Sat in chairs. Listened.

Everything was as it should be.

But the staircase banister was smoother than she remembered. She rubbed her hand along it again. She had scuffed it years ago moving a bookshelf. The scuff wasn’t there.

She made herself check her phone. The date. May 17th. Tuesday. 10:42 p.m.

The clock on the stove read 10:42 p.m. too.

Nothing was wrong.

She went back to the hallway mirror.

She stared. Her reflection stared. She waved. It waved.

She blinked.

Her reflection did not.

It stared back, unblinking.

Then, slowly, it smiled.

Not maliciously. Not cruelly. Almost… gently. As if to say: I understand.

Then it blinked.

Perfectly in sync.

The smile faded.

Marjorie backed away. Just a step. Her heart was beating too fast now.

She went to the front door. She unlocked it, opened it.

The night outside was empty. No wind. No crickets. Not even the hum of the distant highway that usually hung like a low note in the background. Just the still air, and the dark, and a faint, almost imperceptible scent she couldn't place. Not unpleasant. Just… unfamiliar.

She closed the door again.

Back in the kitchen, she opened the junk drawer one more time. It slid out like silk. Inside were the scissors, the lighter, a calculator, a spare key. And a small, round stone she had never seen before — pale gray with a single black stripe running through it like ink.

She picked it up. It was warm.

She put it back.

She considered calling someone. But what would she say?

Hi, I think my house might be the same house but not exactly?
Hi, my reflection doesn’t always match me anymore?
Hi, I think I accidentally slipped into the version of my life where everything is incrementally off and I’m the only one who notices?

She didn’t call.

Instead, she went to bed.

And in the morning, everything was exactly as it had never been.

“What Comes Before”

The first to notice was Mrs. Ellery, the retired schoolteacher who walked her dog at sunrise. She told the grocer that she knew what the weather would be before she opened her curtains. “It’s like I remembered the rain, even though it hadn’t started yet,” she said, her face creased with uneasy amusement.

No one paid it much mind. Everyone in Sycamore Hill had felt déjà vu before. It was just one of those sleepy-town quirks—weathered benches in the park, the smell of cut grass, routine conversations that looped so often they could pass as prophecy.

But it grew.

People began finishing each other’s sentences with unsettling precision. Neighbors paused mid-step and turned around before someone called their name. “Funny, I could’ve sworn I already saw this,” they’d mutter, blinking down the street like it had been dressed twice.

Children started reciting answers in class before questions were asked. Mr. Truan, the mailman, would deliver letters people hadn’t yet written. “No return address,” he’d say. “But I remembered it on your kitchen table.”

The town librarian, Anna Chen, began keeping a journal—not of what had happened, but what would. At first, it was small things: a dropped glass at the diner, a power outage on 3rd Street. But then she started dating each entry as if it were hindsight.

And then she stopped coming in.

That was when people began to remember things that shouldn’t be remembered.

A boy named David swore he remembered failing a math test he hadn’t yet taken. His teacher, confused, told him he had nothing to worry about—it was still a week away. But David began to cry uncontrollably. Not because he feared failing, but because in the memory, he could feel the despair of already having failed—the sick weight of disappointment in his stomach like a meal turned to stone.

Soon, these memories stopped being about the future. They were in the future. People lay awake at night remembering moments from next week. A power outage. A quarrel. A lonely dinner eaten in silence. Losses that hadn’t happened yet, but somehow had.

Then came the funeral.

It was Margaret Pace who told the town council, her voice trembling in the community center. “It was mine,” she said. “I remember the way the lilies smelled. I remember my sister crying, even though she never cries. I remember—my mouth. It was sewn shut.”

A silence passed between the townsfolk like a cold wind. No one spoke for long minutes.

The worst part wasn’t that Margaret believed it was real.

The worst part was that so did everyone else. Not because they had seen it, but because now, they remembered it too.

One by one, others began to remember their own funerals. Always vivid. Always detailed. Embalming fluid. Whispered eulogies. The slamming of car doors in the rain. The texture of closed eyelids. It was as if their minds had reached beyond their span and retrieved something they were never meant to hold.

No one knew when it would happen. Only that it would.

The town began to quiet. People stopped making plans. Why celebrate a birthday when you already remembered the silence after it ended? Why fall in love, when you remembered the last fight, the empty bed, the papers unsigned on the kitchen counter?

Weeks passed. The air in Sycamore Hill became heavy with a stillness that felt like waiting.

And then Anna Chen’s journal reappeared—on the steps of the library, wrapped in brown paper. The last entry was dated tomorrow.

It read:

“They say we’re remembering the future.
But what if it isn’t the future at all?

What if it’s after?

What if these aren't memories of what’s to come,
but echoes from what’s already passed?

What if we’ve all already died—
and this is the flicker of thought that burns in the mind
just before it goes out?

A town caught in the last neuron’s flash.
A moment remembering itself,
again and again,
until the lights go dark.”

Not a future approaching.

But a past exhaling one final breath.

Morning came—and with it, a terrible stillness.

No birds.
No footsteps.
No memory of waking.

Only silence.
And the uncanny knowledge—settling into every empty street and shuttered window—that whatever came before was over.

And what came after—

had already come.

milk—cinnamon—plums—avocados—us?

Not hers.
His.

He showed up at my porch with a little paper bag and that look he gets when he’s about to evangelize. I know it well; it’s the same one he had at six when he tried to convince me that pants were “oppressive.”

First off: no buttons. Not one. Just a piece of glass. You touch it, it buzzes. You don’t touch it, it buzzes anyway. I tried to answer a call by tapping it like Theo said, and I accidentally opened something called TikTok, where a teenage boy was dancing in his kitchen with dead eyes like he was being held hostage by rhythm.

“Swipe up!” Theo yelled, like we were on fire.

Theo said, “You’ll get used to it, Nana.”

Which is what men always say when they hand you something that doesn’t work the way it should.

Now the texting. Oh, the texting. The keyboard is the size of a Chiclet, and the space bar is a liar. Every time I try to write “Hello, this is Eleanor,” I end up with “HellthisisElephant.” Why is the “period” hidden under three menus like it’s ashamed of itself? Punctuation should be proud! I once gave a student detention for writing an essay without a single comma. Her name was Bethany, and she’s in real estate now, which feels about right.

Title: "The Letter with the Red Thread"

The old woman sat hunched on the velvet footstool, a wooden box in her lap. Dust floated lazily in the warm afternoon light, and the lace curtains moved just barely, as if holding their breath. Her hands, bent and blue-veined, lifted the lid slowly.

“Come here, Eliza,” she said, her voice low and papery, but steady. The girl, barely ten, slid to the floor beside her, cross-legged, hair still damp from the bath, and leaned into her grandmother’s side.

Inside were letters—dozens—bundled in twine or ribbon, some yellowed, others still crisp, a few sealed with wax long broken. But one sat alone. No envelope. Folded once, the crease soft with age. A red thread was tied around it, loose and fraying.

The old woman untied it with a tenderness Eliza noticed, and unfolded the letter in her lap.

“I want to read you this one tonight,” she said. “Not for sleep, darling, but for remembering. Even things you don’t know you’re remembering yet.”

She began:

Dear Sarah,

It’s been twenty years, and I still return to that summer we were seventeen. I wonder if you do too. The way the meadow looked that morning—the one near Miller’s Creek where we swore we heard a whippoorwill, though Mama said it was just a mourning dove.

But this isn't about birds. This is about the day you dared me to climb the water tower.

Do you remember? It was July and everything was too hot to move, but you wouldn’t let the heat stop you from doing something “unforgettable.” I hated heights. Still do. But I followed you.

Halfway up, I paused. I made the mistake of looking down. My knees went loose, and I clung to the metal rung like it was the only real thing in the world. I said I couldn’t go farther.

And you looked down at me, all freckles and fearless grin, and said, “Then don’t look down. Look at me instead.”

"Unraveling"

They sat in the lawyer’s office, not touching. The air smelled like laminate wood and old coffee. A glossy stack of papers lay between them — the legal dissociation of a life once held in common. She scrolled absentmindedly through her phone; he traced a blister on his thumb with his other hand. No eye contact. No words. Just the soft skritch of the lawyer’s pen, parsing their history into property, custody, debt.

The silence between them wasn’t angry. That would’ve been easier. It was the silence of two people who had once known each other’s morning breath, the pace of each heartbeat, the depth of each wound — and now couldn’t summon anything to say. That forgetting had taken years. It wore a thousand disguises.

Two weeks earlier, they’d sat across the kitchen table with shadows under their eyes. She was holding a chipped mug with both hands. He kept opening his mouth as if about to speak, but saying nothing. When she finally said, “I think we need to talk,” his shoulders dropped in relief and sorrow, like a man surrendering to a truth he’d already memorized.

They had fought less and less in the past year. Disagreements had hollowed out into shrugs. Words became blunt, dull tools. She used to cry after arguments — now she just stared through him, like he’d become a room to walk through on her way elsewhere.

Last summer, they tried to fix things. They had taken a trip to the coast — the same beach where he had proposed under a sky that wouldn't stop raining. They took long walks. Read side by side. Made love in the thin motel bed and held each other afterward like survivors.

But even those moments had a brittle edge. He turned away quickly in sleep. She watched the tide go in and out and felt she was standing still, waist-deep in something she couldn't name. At dinner, they laughed about one thing or another — she showed him a meme, he teased her about her obsession with tiny spoons — but somehow the laughter left no trace behind. It echoed too fast.

A year before that, their daughter had started kindergarten. He cried more than she did. He had packed her tiny lunch and slipped a note inside it: You are braver than you think. She called him afterward and they both chuckled at how grown-up their daughter looked with her backpack bigger than her torso. That night, after their daughter had fallen asleep clutching a glittery dinosaur, they lay in bed listening to her soft snoring.

He whispered, “We made a person.”

She smiled and pressed her face into his chest, her hand slipping under his t-shirt to rest over his heart.

Their small apartment had been loud in those early years — not with anger, but with life. Music while they cooked, voices crossed over each other, the rhythmic argument of who did or didn’t take out the garbage. There were tears then, too, but they always ended in pulling each other close under blankets, mumbling apologies into collarbones.

When he lost his job and went quiet for a month, she made him get up every morning, drive with her to work, and sit in the cafe next door, just to keep moving. He hated the coffee there. She ordered it for him anyway. "You'll survive," she said, with a crooked smile. He had.

Their wedding was in a park, under a hot sky. Her dress caught on everything. His tie was slightly crooked. The ceremony was short, the vows a little rushed, but the look in their eyes — like they were standing at the edge of the world and daring it to end — made even the minister stumble. She dropped the ring during the exchange. They both laughed so hard they had to pause the ceremony. Everyone clapped.

That night, they lay on the floor eating leftover cake with their fingers, him licking icing off her wrist.

“If you ever leave me,” she said, “I get the dog. And the dish towels.”

“You have weird priorities,” he teased.

“You have no taste in dish towels,” she replied, and he kissed her like he’d never need to breathe again.

Before that, there were long nights of planning a shared life: where they’d live, whether they wanted kids, how they’d handle money and Christmas visits and the fear of getting too comfortable. They promised to let each other grow. They promised to fight fair. They said impossible things, like forever, and only you, and whatever happens, we’ll talk about it.

Before that, there were firsts: the first I love you, stammered during a drunk cab ride and then panicked over for days. The first serious argument, when she walked out into the cold and he followed five minutes later, holding her coat like a peace offering. The first time she saw him crying quietly while watching a movie and realized, in her bones, I could spend my life with you.

And before all that, that very first moment.

A bookstore, late afternoon. Rain on the glass. She was standing in the poetry section, pulling down a slim blue volume of Rilke. He reached for the same book, their hands touching.

“Sorry,” he said.

“No, go ahead,” she replied, but smiled.

He made some offhand joke about Rilke being too tragic for a rainy day, and she replied with a line from the Duino Elegies that made him pause.

They stood there for a while — two strangers, both pretending not to be looking for something. Then he said, “Want to get coffee?” and she said yes before she even thought about it.

She would tell her friends later that something about his eyes made her feel understood.

He would tell his brother that she smelled like rain and paper and that for the first time in years, he felt… lucky.

And there, where it all began — before the phone bills and the disappointments and the silence in the lawyer's office — there was just the quiet miracle of two people choosing each other, not yet knowing how hard it would be to carry love forward, not yet knowing how exquisitely it could hurt to remember the beginning after the end.

"The Seeds We Keep"

Now

The spade sinks easily into the loam. It has rained last night—the good kind of rain, slow and steady, the kind the earth accepts without resistance. She presses her boot down and feels the give of the soil, a soft sigh rising with the scent of earth.

Around her, the garden stirs—bare rows of dark dirt, waiting. She kneels, brushing hair from her face with a dirt-smeared hand, and separates the seed packets: tomatoes, peas, marigolds for the borders. She doesn't plant in straight lines. She never could. The carrots will wander. The basil will push up wherever it likes.

She tucks the seeds in like small secrets.

Then

Her knees are muddy. Her father told her not to kneel but crouch, so she doesn’t smother the soil. “It needs to breathe,” he’d said, his voice low and gravelly as though he were speaking to the dirt itself.

She watches him make a furrow with the edge of his hand, the motion repetitive, meditative. She tries to mimic it, but her lines wobble, stray. He watches, and instead of correcting her, he offers a slight nod.

"Plants don’t mind a little chaos," he says, and moves on.

She’s seven, and she doesn’t understand most of what he says. But she holds onto this one.

Now

The gloves stay off today. She wants to feel everything—the rough husk of the pea pods as she presses them down, the wet coolness that clings to her palms. A robin sings from the fence post, and for a moment something sharp rises in her chest, something that arrives without name.

The fence is new. The old one fell last winter, bent under snow and time. She rebuilt it last month, post by post, the hammer swinging in rhythm with remembered sounds.

She murmurs to the peas as she plants them. It's not words exactly, more the rhythm of voice. They deserve a welcome.

Then

They've just come back from the nursery. Her father carries the flats of seedlings like sacred things. His hands, thick and calloused, cradle the trays as if they’re made of glass. She tries to carry one too, but the tomato plant tips, and she stumbles. A dark chunk of soil hits the ground.

She waits for him to scold her. He doesn’t. Instead, he picks up the plant gently, brushes off the roots, and says, “It’ll recover. They’re tougher than they look.”

She isn’t sure if he’s still talking about tomatoes.

Now

The sun is high now, climbing soft and certain. The first row is done. There’s dirt beneath her fingernails and a blister starting on her right thumb. She smiles without meaning to.

Behind her, the house stands quiet. Its windows are open. The kitchen curtains breathe in and out. Somewhere inside, the kettle whistles and then silences itself. There is no rush. Everything she needs is already here.

She presses one last seed into the soil, almost ceremonially, then smooths the ground over with the side of her hand. A small goodbye, a small beginning.

Then

He lets her water the garden when they’re done. The hose snakes between the rows, and she holds the nozzle too tightly at first, splashing dirt onto the paths. He laughs—a sound she won’t hear much in the years to come—and adjusts her grip.

"Like this," he says, guiding her hand. "Let it rain slow. Let it sink in before you give it more."

She watches as the water darkens the soil, sees how it drinks from the sky. She will remember this.

Later, she sits in the swing beneath the maple tree, bare feet caked in mud, the garden behind her humming with its silent promises. He is beside her, tired but content, a lemonade bottle sweating in his hand.

They don’t speak. They don’t need to.

Now

She sits in the same swing, now worn soft by years. Her boots sit beside her, empty. The garden stretches ahead, rows not straight but sure. A wind stirs the leaves of the maple overhead, and she leans back, eyes half-closed, listening to the hush of green things growing.

Deep in the dirt, the seeds remember.

In six months, the town of Windlow would be gone. The river had been marked for damming, and the valley would become a reservoir deep enough to swallow rooftops, barns, and gravestones. The government flyers said progress was coming. The engineers nodded solemnly. But maps didn't show the smell of rain on Main Street, or the way light poured over the fields like syrup in October. Still, the timeline was set. On February 12th, the dam would close, and the water would rise. Everyone had their deadline. Everyone but Nathan Mearns.

Nathan was fifty-eight and a woodworker by trade, though the word “trade” didn’t quite fit. It was more like devotion, slow and exacting. For the last thirty years, he'd repaired tables, turned cribs into rocking chairs, carved initials into mantlepieces. He lived in a small cottage just off the edge of town. Nothing special, people might’ve said. Not until the day he drew plans for the house he'd never been able to build—his dream house—and began, with stubborn grace, to make it real.

It began with the foundation, laid by hand in early August, each stone kissed with mortar under his steady palms. He ignored the sideways glances. "Why now?" some asked gently, as if he didn’t know. Others didn’t ask. They thought it might be a breakdown, some quiet kind of madness. But he kept going, like a man pouring hours into an hourglass he knew was cracked.

The frame rose in September. He cut the beams himself from an old grove outside town, stripped bark with care, sanded the knots until they glowed like scars. He worked without music, without help, just the rhythm of breath and hammer and birdcall.

Neighbors brought him lemonade, at first to talk him down, but then just to watch. There was something holy about it—each nail, each joint, done with the patience of prayer. The house was not large, but it had long windows to catch the western sun, and a porch wide enough for a pair of rocking chairs. A man and a memory, perhaps.

By October, shingles clattered onto the roof. He painted the walls a color he called "milkstone," a pale, whispering gray. Inside, he built a table from cherrywood. No screws, just dovetail joints, smooth and strong. He carved into the leg: For when I remember who I am.

The town began packing: boxes in windows, moving trucks on Sundays. Kids walked slower past Nathan's lot. Something about it sank into them. A kind of ache.

In November, he built the bedroom with a skylight. He lay on the floor one night, the stars just visible through the bare glass. He whispered the names of people who’d been gone a long time—his wife Marie, dead twenty-one years; his mother and father; the old storekeeper who used to give him licorice as a boy. Maybe he'd conjure them, just for a moment. Maybe they'd sit with him on the porch, sipping silence.

December came cruel and bright. Snow limned the roof like icing. He cooked his meals on a wood stove he'd salvaged, sat at the cherrywood table, and watched the shadows move across the floorboards. The house creaked like it was learning his name.

On the first of February, he planted a dogwood tree outside the front window. He knew it wouldn’t bloom. He planted it anyway.

The night before the flood, he sat on the porch with a cup of black coffee. He looked at the sky, then at the line of hills that would soon be islands. The house stood behind him, warm and real, held together by hands and memory.

No one saw him leave. But he left the door unlocked, the fire banked low, the bed made.

When the waters came, they rose slow and patient, like they respected what they'd take. The reservoir swallowed Windlow by inches, until only the hills knew what lay beneath.

They say the house is still down there, whole and undrowned, a breath held tight in the lungs of the earth. When divers go over the spot in spring, they claim they feel something—a stillness, a hush. Like walking into a chapel built not for saving, but for remembering.

And somewhere in silt and silence, a table waits for supper, lit by nothing but memory.

Title: "A Sudden Impact"

1. Lila – The Driver Who Caused It

I swear, I looked. I did. The light was yellow, and I knew I had time—I thought I did. My phone buzzed in the cupholder, and I glanced down. Maybe half a second. Maybe less. When I looked up, there she was, in the intersection, headlights too close. I slammed on the brakes, but I was still moving at least thirty. The sound—metal on metal, glass, screams—I don't think I'll ever lose it.

I got out, shaking, knees jelly. Her car was crumpled on the passenger side. It looked like a can crushed under a shoe. She wasn’t moving. People were yelling. I kept saying, “I’m sorry! She ran the red, right? Didn’t she run it?” Someone said, “You did.” And I felt my stomach drop, like I’d just been pushed off a cliff.

But I know I had the light. I know I did.

2. Marcus – The Driver Who Was Hit

I was driving back from my sister’s place. We’d been fighting earlier in the week, and tonight we patched things up. She packed me some leftovers in Tupperware; the bag rode shotgun like a passenger. I was smiling like an idiot.

The light was green. There was no ambiguity. No blinking yellow, no stale color. Just green. I eased into the intersection, not too fast.

Then—bam. A blur, then pain. Glass shattered into my face like a thousand needles. I tasted blood, metallic and warm. I couldn’t move my left arm. A voice inside kept saying, You’re alive. Don’t move. Don’t die. Don’t move.

It never occurred to me, not once, that I could have been in the wrong.

3. Rosa – The Pedestrian Who Witnessed It

I walk that corner every evening after work. Thirty years, same route. I wait for the little white man to blink on and I cross Maple. That night, I was standing at the curb, listening to some podcast about crime statistics in Detroit, of all things.

That’s when I saw her—this little sedan, silver. It wasn’t speeding, but it wasn’t slowing down either. The light turned red for her—I saw it—and she went through like it was still hers. The other car was already in motion, entering on a green. No way he could’ve stopped in time.

I remember yelling, instinctively. Like yelling would stop them. After the crash, I ran over. The girl—it was a girl, twenty-something—kept saying she had the green. But I saw it. I saw her run the red.

Funny thing, though—I also saw her glance down. Like, just before she entered the intersection. She looked down, then up, like she was replying to a text. If she’d looked sooner, maybe she would’ve stopped. Maybe that fraction of a second would’ve made the difference.

4. Darren – The EMT Who Arrived Three Minutes Later

Call came in as a two-car T-bone, possible entrapment. I was two blocks away. When I pulled up, the smell hit me—burnt rubber, leaking coolant, adrenaline in the air like ozone before a storm.

My partner went to the woman in the silver sedan. Conscious, hyperventilating, a thousand-yard stare. I checked the guy in the dark blue Civic. Mid-thirties, semi-conscious, left humerus broken for sure. No head trauma, thank God.

As I stabilized him, I noticed something strange. On the passenger seat, under a blanket, was a baby carrier. Empty. But the straps were buckled, like something had been in it recently. I called over: “Any kids involved?”

“No kid,” someone said. “He was alone.”

Then I found the Tupperware in the footwell—split open, mango chutney everywhere. Smelled like home, like comfort.

I was about to close the door to prep the ride when I heard a woman, a pedestrian, talking to a cop. She said the girl ran the red. That she was looking down.

I turned to look at the girl again. She was crying now, shoulders shaking. Saying, “I looked up. I swear I looked up.”

Maybe she did. Maybe she looked up too late. Or maybe, in her mind, she wanted to have looked up. Shock does that—it rearranges your memory like furniture in the dark.

Truth is, accidents don’t always have villains. Just people, split-second decisions, and a timing the universe doesn't forgive.

But the light was red. And phones don’t help.

Truth in the Cracks:

Lila believed she had the light—her brain, fogged by distraction and adrenaline, rewrote the moment to protect her.
Marcus was sure he was innocent, and he was, mostly. But maybe he didn’t ease in as slowly as he thought.
Rosa saw the red, clear as day—but only by chance, only because she was waiting to cross and happened to glance up.
And Darren, trained to stabilize broken bodies, pieced together the emotional fragments: the baby carrier, the forgotten dinner, the tear-streaked confession of a girl who would carry this one second with her forever.

Each saw a sliver.

Each was right.

And yet, only together do they tell the full, raw, human truth.
